nodes.label: Theorem 14.1 — X Is Closed iff X = R(X)
nodes.rationale: Stated as not new mathematics, and the book gains by saying so: it is Bergman's double-projection theorem specialised to products of chains, itself a consequence of Baker and Pixley (1975) for any algebra with a majority term. What follows is that E(Lambda) = 0 is the statement that Lambda is a sublattice.

nodes.label: Prior Owners — Global Consistency and the Staircase Class
nodes.rationale: E(X) = 0 is global consistency of a binary constraint network certified by Montanari (1974) and Dechter (1992), and the constraint class has a name — the staircase / connected row-convex class of Deville, Bartak and Van Hentenryck (1999) — so the operator has been building a named object since Chapter 6.

nodes.label: R Is a Closure Operator; E(X) Is a Closure Defect
nodes.rationale: Extensive, monotone and idempotent exhaustively, so E(X) is a standard object from Galois theory, formal concept analysis and database dependency theory; no novelty is claimed for the machinery, only for computing the closure defect of an index — the periodic table's is 36, Lambda's 0.

nodes.label: The Scope — Coordinates Must Be Presented as Chains
nodes.rationale: Requiring each coordinate be presented as a chain is not requiring the factors to be chains: any distributive factor can be so presented via Birkhoff. What fails is bundling, because R reconstructs coordinate by coordinate, so folding two chains into one non-chain coordinate hides structure from it.

nodes.label: The Closed Sets Form a Moore Family
nodes.rationale: Closed under intersection, containing the whole index, not closed under union — the standard fact about any closure operator, worth stating because the asymmetry is R's own one level up: R carries meets and refuses joins and its fixed points do the same, 100% against 32-68%.

nodes.label: Lambda Is the Closure of Seven of Its Cells
nodes.rationale: Reading envelope steps as elements and cells as covering sets makes the seed a minimum set cover, which is what makes seven exact rather than approximate — a lower bound met, not a heuristic's best attempt. Seven beats Birkhoff's seventeen because R fills the envelope box where the lattice join reaches only the down-set.

nodes.label: The Seed as a Caratheodory Number
The Seed Is Linear in Dimension and the Index Is Not
nodes.rationale: seed = Caratheodory number + alphabet cost, the breadth plus one witness per value no envelope step supplies; the seed cannot be constant because a generating set must reach the breadth of what it generates. The law holds while the tower adds counting axes and breaks where it begins coupling — the dichotomy seen in a third quantity.

nodes.label: A Stable Core With Nothing Forced
nodes.rationale: No envelope element is covered by exactly one cell, at any cap setting or at Lambda_9, so the four recurring corners are a stable attractor of greedy covering rather than a forced core; 519 completing triples across 66 cells make every position recoverable and there is no critical core.

nodes.label: The Constraint Is on the Channel, Not the Cell
nodes.rationale: Across 219 distinct minimum covers, six channel conditions hold in every one — s->s, s->p, p->s, p->p, a null transfer and a full transfer — which is exactly why no single element is uniquely covered while every cover looks alike.

nodes.label: The Fifth Position — The Cell That Carries the Unit
nodes.rationale: The four corners are extremal on every coordinate they fix and none carries the value one; the fifth cell's function is to supply it, and its single free coordinate is a fork between witnessing the target's ceiling or the source's.

nodes.label: The Seed as Five Words in Which Every Letter Is Spoken Both Ways
nodes.rationale: Every one of the eight coordinates receives both a 0 and a 1 across the five cells, which is what a covering set of envelope steps must do, made visible as a bit table; the complementary pairing is measured at one cap setting and is flagged as a described property rather than a structural law.
